vignette:
She is a 75-year-old Oceania woman who has spent most of her life in steady work and careful routines, and in the early years she would have described herself as practical, observant, and hard to unsettle. As an auditor, she has long been the person who notices what does not add up. Numbers, receipts, and records once gave her a sense that the world could be made orderly if one looked closely enough. Even now, in her marriage, she tends to be the one who keeps track of bills, appointments, and the small details of daily life. She speaks with the composed precision of someone used to accountability, but underneath that composure there is a constant vigilance that did not used to be there.

The traumatic events begin when she is living as a civilian in a war zone, trying to maintain ordinary life while the country around her is breaking apart. At first, she tells herself that the shelling is distant, that the streets will calm again, that the next day will be like the one before. She continues to go to work because work feels like proof that life remains intact. But the attacks move closer, and one day she is caught in a sudden barrage that turns familiar sounds into something lethal. She remembers the blast more than anything else: the brutal impact, the dust, the confusion of people screaming and running in different directions, the sickening sense that the ground itself is unsafe. She does not know if she is injured at first; she only knows she cannot think clearly, cannot get her bearings, cannot make the world line up the way it should.

Afterward, she becomes preoccupied with small practical tasks because they are the only things she can still control. She checks doors and windows repeatedly. She inventories food, water, documents, and medicines with the same exactness she once brought to ledgers at work. During the worst periods, she hears sudden noises as if they are coming again, and her body responds before her mind can catch up. A car backfiring, a slamming door, even a heavy book dropped on the floor can send her heart racing and leave her shaky for minutes afterward. She starts scanning the sky, the street, the faces of strangers. She notices exits wherever she goes. If there is a crowd, she stands where she can see everyone and move quickly if necessary.

She eventually leaves the war zone, but leaving does not end the war inside her. In the years that follow, she builds a life that looks calm from the outside. She marries, works, and raises the appearance of normalcy with the same discipline she once used to survive. Yet she remains organized around threat. She avoids war films, news reports, and even certain conversations because anything that resembles the past can pull her back into it. When she does sleep, she has dreams that are not always exact memories but carry the same terror: she is searching for shelter, cannot find her family, or is trapped while explosions come closer. She wakes disoriented and often cannot return to sleep. Her husband has learned that some nights she rises quietly and checks the locks, then sits in the dark trying to steady herself without waking him.

Her memory of the trauma is not only vivid; it is intrusive in a way that feels involuntary and humiliating. At times, a smell of smoke or diesel catches her by surprise and she is suddenly back in the war zone, feeling the same pressure in her chest and the same dread that someone will not make it in time. She becomes irritable in a way she does not like in herself. She snaps at small interruptions, then feels guilty and exhausted afterward. She is often tense in her shoulders and jaw, as if bracing for impact. Crowded supermarkets, sirens, and loud motorcycles leave her drained. She prefers sitting with her back to a wall, watching the room rather than participating in it.

Over time, she notices that parts of herself have gone quiet. She feels less able to experience ease, and moments that should be pleasant often register only faintly. She still functions, still works with numbers and records, but the work now serves another purpose: it keeps her occupied enough not to think. Even there, she has become more cautious, rereading figures more often than before and double-checking tasks because mistakes feel dangerous in a world that once fell apart without warning. She describes herself as living “half in the present and half somewhere else,” as if a part of her never fully returned from the days when every sound might mean death.
